title: Reciprocal translocation t(9;22)
clinical_history: A 48-year-old man has fatigue, splenomegaly, and marked leukocytosis with a left shift. Bone marrow cytogenetic analysis is requested. This is an acquired (cancer) cytogenetics teaching case, not a constitutional study.
unknown_prompt: An adult with leukocytosis and splenomegaly undergoes bone marrow karyotyping. Identify any structural rearrangement, write the ISCN, and name the associated neoplasm. Chromosome images are demonstration schematics.
plain_language_interpretation: A male karyotype with 46 chromosomes and a reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, with breakpoints at 9q34 and 22q11.2. The derivative chromosome 22 is the Philadelphia chromosome.
explanation: The t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) reciprocal translocation generates der(9) and der(22). The small der(22) is the Philadelphia chromosome and juxtaposes BCR at 22q11.2 with ABL1 at 9q34, producing BCR::ABL1. This acquired abnormality is the cytogenetic hallmark of chronic myeloid leukemia and also occurs in a subset of ALL. It is not a Robertsonian translocation; Robertsonian rearrangements involve whole-arm exchanges between acrocentric chromosomes at q10. In ISCN the balanced translocation is written t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) after the sex-chromosome complement.
hints: The count remains 46. Look at chromosomes 9 and 22 rather than searching for an extra G-group chromosome.
One chromosome 22 is unusually small (the Philadelphia chromosome, der(22)). One chromosome 9 q arm is altered.
Reciprocal translocations are written t(A;B)(breakpointA;breakpointB) with chromosomes in ascending numerical order.
